Yes, there is a real difference. `RUN cd /` has **no lasting effect**, while `WORKDIR /` changes the working directory for everything that follows.

## `RUN cd /`

Each `RUN` instruction runs in its own shell process inside a temporary container. Docker then commits the resulting **filesystem changes** as a new layer.

The current directory belongs to the shell process, not the filesystem. When the process exits, the `cd` is lost. So:

```dockerfile
RUN cd /tmp
RUN pwd          # prints "/" (or whatever WORKDIR is), NOT /tmp
```

`RUN cd /` on its own is effectively a no-op. It only adds a build step (and an empty layer/history entry).

It *is* useful when chained within the same `RUN`:

```dockerfile
RUN cd /src && make && make install
```

Here the `cd` affects only the commands in that one shell invocation.

## `WORKDIR /`

`WORKDIR` is a Dockerfile instruction that sets the working directory in the **image's configuration (metadata)**. It persists and affects:

- all subsequent `RUN`, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT`, `COPY`, and `ADD` instructions in the Dockerfile
- containers started from the image. `docker run` and `docker exec` start in that directory unless overridden with `-w`/`--workdir`
- child images built `FROM` this image, which inherit it

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /tmp
RUN pwd          # prints /tmp
COPY foo.txt .   # copies to /tmp/foo.txt
CMD ["pwd"]      # container prints /tmp
```

Other `WORKDIR` behaviors:
- **It creates the directory** if it doesn't exist (`RUN cd /nonexistent` would fail).
- **Relative paths stack** on the previous `WORKDIR`:
  ```dockerfile
  WORKDIR /a
  WORKDIR b
  WORKDIR c
  RUN pwd   # /a/b/c
  ```
- **It expands variables** set with `ENV`:
  ```dockerfile
  ENV APP=/opt/app
  WORKDIR $APP
  ```

## Summary

| | `RUN cd /` | `WORKDIR /` |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Only within that single `RUN` shell | All later instructions and the running container |
| Stored in image config | No | Yes |
| Creates missing directory | No (fails) | Yes |
| Affects `COPY`/`ADD`/`CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` | No | Yes |

**Best practice** (per Docker's docs): use `WORKDIR` to set directories instead of `RUN cd … && …` chains. It's clearer, more reliable, and easier to maintain.

Yes, there's a real difference. `RUN cd /` does almost nothing useful. `WORKDIR /` changes the directory for everything that comes after it.

## Why `RUN cd` doesn't stick

Each `RUN` line starts a fresh shell in a temporary container. When that shell exits, its current directory is gone. So the next instruction starts back in whatever the working directory was before.

```dockerfile
RUN cd /tmp
RUN pwd        # prints "/", not "/tmp"
```

The `cd` only lasts for the rest of that one `RUN` line. That's why you often see it chained:

```dockerfile
RUN cd /tmp && make && make install
```

## What `WORKDIR` does

`WORKDIR` sets the working directory for every instruction after it, until another `WORKDIR` changes it:

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /tmp
RUN pwd        # prints "/tmp"
COPY . .       # copies into /tmp
```

It applies to `RUN`, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT`, `COPY`, and `ADD`.

## Other differences

- **It carries into the running container.** `WORKDIR` is saved in the image's config. When you `docker run` the image, you start in that directory. `RUN cd` has no effect at runtime.
- **It creates the directory if it doesn't exist.** `RUN cd /foo` fails if `/foo` isn't there.
- **Relative paths build on each other.**
  ```dockerfile
  WORKDIR /a
  WORKDIR b
  WORKDIR c
  RUN pwd      # /a/b/c
  ```
- **It can use `ENV` variables**, like `WORKDIR $APP_HOME`.
- **No shell needed.** `WORKDIR` is handled by Docker itself. `RUN cd` needs a shell in the image, so it won't work in something like a `scratch` image.

## Rule of thumb

Use `WORKDIR` when you want to change directory for later steps or for the container. Use `cd` only inside a single `RUN` that chains several commands together.

### Why Example 2 is a bug waiting to happen

```bash

ok() {
  if [ -n "$A" ]; then
    local animal
    animal="zebra"
  fi
  animal="lion"      # later code in the same function

}

ok            # prints: lion

```

Because the `if` branch didn't run, `local animal` never executed. The later assignment modified the **global** variable. With Example 1 this can't happen:

```bash

  local animal       # always executes, so animal is always local

  if [ -n "$A" ]; then
    animal="zebra"
  fi
  animal="lion"
  echo "$animal"
}
```

```bash

  local name count result
  local -a items
  local -i total=0

  # ... logic ...
}
```

Declaring everything at the top:
- guarantees the variables are local no matter which branch runs
- documents the function's variables in one place
- matches how bash actually scopes variables

### Related gotcha: `local` with command substitution

```bash
local out=$(some_command)   # $? is the exit status of `local`, which is always 0
```

Separate the declaration from the assignment if you need the exit status:

```bash

out=$(some_command) || return 1
```


In Bash:

2. **`local` takes effect only when it runs.** It is an ordinary builtin executed at runtime, not something the parser sees in advance. From the moment it runs until the function returns, the variable is local to the function, even outside the `if` block. That's why Example 2 printed `zebra`.

## Demonstration of the bug

```bash

ok() {
  if [ -n "$A" ]; then
    local animal
    animal="zebra"
  fi
  animal="lion"       # author assumes this is local...
}

A=""                  # condition is false, so `local` never runs
ok
```

With Example 1's style, the global stays `cat` no matter which branch runs:

```bash
  fi
  animal="lion"

```

## Dynamic scoping makes this worse

Bash uses dynamic scoping. A function you call can see and modify your locals, and if you forget to make something local, you can overwrite a variable belonging to whoever called you, not just a global:

```bash

outer() {
  local result="outer's value"
  inner
  echo "$result"                   # prints "from inner"
}
outer
```

This is another reason to declare every function variable as `local`, unconditionally, at the start of the function.

## Recommended style

```bash

  local animal
  local count=0
  local file
```

The Python community now has several popular packaging tools. `setuptools` still appears to be the most widely used, but it is no longer the de facto standard. This causes several problems for both end users and developers:

- For `setuptools`-based packages, installing from source or building a distribution can fail if `setuptools` isn't installed.
- `pip` can't install packages from source when they rely on other packaging tools. Those tools therefore had to generate a `setup.py` file to produce a compatible package. To build a distribution package, you first have to install the packaging tool and then run its own commands.
- If a package's author switches to a different packaging tool, workflows also have to change to use that tool's commands.

Any tool may also add its own section (table) to this file for tool-specific options. Doing so is up to each tool and isn't mandatory.

Like state updates in class components that extend React.Component or React.PureComponent, updates made with the useState updater are asynchronous and won't show up immediately.

The bigger issue, though, is that functions use the state values from the closure they were created in. A state update takes effect on the next re-render, and that re-render doesn't change existing closures. It creates new ones. So a function keeps seeing the values from its old closure until the component re-renders and the function is recreated, or not, depending on how it was defined.

Adding a timeout doesn't fix this. The timeout may fire after the re-render has happened, but the callback still reads the value from its original closure, not the updated one.

If you want to do something once the state has updated, use the useEffect hook, similar to using a componentDidUpdate-style callback in class components. The setter returned by useState doesn't accept a callback, so this is the right approach.

As for updating the state itself, a plain set call replaces the previous value with the data from the async request. If you want to merge the response into the existing values, use the callback form of the setter, which receives the previous state, and combine it with the spread syntax.

Both are commonly used to supply a default when the first value is missing. However, the OR operator can cause trouble if the left value might be one of the falsy values, since those would trigger the fallback even though they are legitimate values.

If you only want the fallback when the left value is null or undefined, the nullish coalescing operator is the right tool.

The operator isn't available in the current LTS versions of Node (v10 and v12), but you can use it with certain versions of TypeScript or Node. It was added in TypeScript 3.7, released in November 2019. More recently, it became part of ES2020, which Node 14 (released in April 2020) supports.

With the fast-forward-only option, Git updates your branch only if it can be fast-forwarded without creating new commits. If that isn't possible, the command stops with an error message.

The warning was added in Git 2.27.

The complete warning offers three options. Each one suppresses the warning, but they serve different purposes:

- **Merge:** Keeps the default behavior and suppresses the warning.
- **Rebase:** Commits your work on top of the remote branch, so you keep a single branch both locally and remotely. The default behavior instead involves two diverged branches that are combined with a merge.
- **Fast-forward only:** Pulls only if the local branch can be fast-forwarded. Otherwise it aborts with an error and creates no commits.

In Git 2.29 and later, you can set the pull behavior configuration to the mode you want, which also removes the warning. The modes are:

- The default: fast-forward when possible, otherwise merge.
- Never fast-forward. A merge is always created.
- Fast-forward when possible, otherwise abort with an error message.

By default, `git pull` performs a merge, and that merge frequently produces a merge commit. So pulling from the remote isn't automatically a harmless action: it can introduce a commit SHA hash that wasn't there before. That can be confusing, since something that feels like a simple download ends up altering your commit history in ways you didn't anticipate.

To prevent this, you need `git pull --ff-only`. (Or maybe not. Keep reading to figure out which option suits you.)

With `git pull --ff-only`, Git updates your branch only when it can be "fast-forwarded" without making any new commits. When that isn't possible, Git just stops and prints an error.

If you'd like this to happen even when you forget the flag, you can make it your Git client's default:

```
git config --global pull.ff only
```

Note: `--global` makes the setting apply to every repository on your machine. To limit it to the current repository, leave that flag out.

This warning first appeared in Git 2.27.

The full warning offers three commands, and running any of them will silence it. However, each does something different:

- `git config pull.rebase false` leaves the default behaviour as it is and simply stops the warning.
- `git config pull.rebase true` places your commits on top of the remote branch, so you keep a single branch locally and remotely. By default, by contrast, there are two separate branches (one local, one remote), and a merge is used to bring them together.
- `git config pull.ff only` pulls only when the local branch can be fast-forwarded. Otherwise it stops with an error and creates no commits.

On Git 2.29 or newer, you can also make the warning go away by setting `pull.ff` to `false`, `true`, or `only`:

- `true`: the default behaviour. The pull fast-forwards when it can and merges when it can't.
- `false`: the pull never fast-forwards and always creates a merge.
- `only`: the pull fast-forwards when it can and otherwise stops with an error.

This explanation compares the Debezium SQL Server CDC Connector with the JDBC Connector, and also offers broader context on Debezium and CDC.

Debezium works only as a source connector and captures every row-level change. According to the Debezium documentation, the Debezium Connector for SQL Server first takes a snapshot of the database and then sends row-level change records to Kafka, with each table going to its own Kafka topic. The Debezium SQL Server connector documentation also covers this.

The Kafka Connect JDBC connector can act as either a source or a sink, and it works with any database that has a JDBC driver. The JDBC Connector documentation describes this. It also includes instructions for installing on Microsoft SQL Server, which I don't think matter for this discussion.

Since the JDBC Connector supports both source and sink roles while Debezium supports only the source role, writing data from Kafka into a JDBC-accessible database (a sink) requires the JDBC Connector, including for SQL Server.

The comparison can therefore be limited to the source side. The JDBC source connector documentation doesn't say much more at first glance, so I looked further. A Debezium blog post uses the Debezium MySQL connector as a source and the JDBC connector as a sink. It explains that Debezium provides records with more detail about database changes, while the JDBC connector provides records focused on turning those changes into simple insert or upsert commands. The two also use different topic naming and different delete handling.

A Confluent blog post explains how CDC and the JDBC connector work. The JDBC connector runs queries against the source database at a fixed interval, which doesn't scale well. CDC runs at a higher frequency by streaming changes from the database transaction log.

Another blog post also contrasts CDC with the JDBC connector. It notes that the JDBC connector doesn't sync deleted records, so it suits prototyping, while CDC suits more mature systems.

The main differences between Debezium and the JDBC Connector are:

- Debezium works only as a Kafka source, while the JDBC Connector can work as either a Kafka source or sink.
- The JDBC Connector doesn't sync deleted records, while Debezium does.
- The JDBC Connector polls the database at a fixed interval, which doesn't scale well. CDC runs at a higher frequency by streaming from the database transaction log.
- Debezium provides records with more information about database changes, while the JDBC Connector provides records focused on converting those changes into simple insert or upsert commands.

According to the Debezium documentation, Debezium works only as a source connector and captures every row-level change.

The Debezium SQL Server Connector documentation explains that the connector begins by taking a snapshot of the database. It then streams row-level change records to Kafka, with each table going to its own Kafka topic.

The JDBC Connector documentation states that Kafka Connect JDBC can act as either a source or a sink connector for Kafka and works with any database that has a JDBC driver. It also includes some notes on installing for Microsoft SQL Server, which I don't consider relevant here.

Because the JDBC Connector handles both source and sink while Debezium handles only source, the JDBC Connector is the choice for writing data from Kafka into any database with a JDBC driver (SQL Server included).

That leaves the comparison to the source side only. At first glance, the JDBC Source Connector documentation doesn't offer much more detail.

Digging further, a Debezium blog post that pairs the Debezium MySQL Connector as the source with the JDBC Connector as the sink explains how the two differ. Broadly, Debezium's records carry more information about the database changes. The JDBC Connector's records concentrate on turning those changes into simple insert/upsert commands. The two also name topics differently and handle deletes differently.

A Confluent blog post describes in more detail how CDC and the JDBC Connector operate. The JDBC Connector runs queries against the source database at a fixed interval, which doesn't scale well. CDC achieves higher frequency by streaming from the database's transaction log.

Another blog post covers the same contrast. Its main point is that the JDBC Connector can't sync deleted records, which makes it suitable for prototyping, whereas CDC suits more mature systems.

- Debezium serves only as a Kafka source, while the JDBC Connector can serve as both a Kafka source and a sink.
- Debezium supports syncing deleted records, while the JDBC Connector does not.
- The JDBC Connector polls the database at a fixed interval, which doesn't scale well. CDC streams from the transaction log at a higher frequency.

There is no direct equivalent, as far as I know. Before getting into specifics, a few points matter when building an application on a PostgreSQL database.

First, it may seem backwards, but you should treat errors from the database as useful. An error only tells you the status of an operation. It doesn't mean the application should crash.

Second, the two cases differ. An insert has a real choice to make, either update the existing row or do nothing, so a syntax that lets you pick makes sense. An update has no such choice. The only thing to do when it conflicts is do nothing, so SQL has no reason to offer a special clause for it. Since the database reporting an error is good, let it do nothing and tell you why.

Third, updating primary keys is bad practice. The insert-time upsert clause isn't meant to change primary key fields. It's meant to update all the non-primary-key fields of a single record.

It's also worth noting that a conflict on the primary key isn't the only way a query can fail. A foreign key constraint could fail a record too, which is still better than silently updating 10M+ records across 50 tables with a ... Also, Oracle doesn't have this clause at all. Why do you think that is?

So what should you do, and what should you avoid?

Don't update primary keys. Your question still applies to other constraints, but please never update primary keys.

Don't check whether a conflicting record exists first. That can be slow and still unreliable. Do you really want to select millions of rows just to avoid an error? And if you extend this to other constraints, will you really write the extra code, only to avoid an error code again? Finally, if you use row-level security, the conflicting row may be one you aren't allowed to see.

Handle the error code in your application. Receiving the status is a good thing.

If you're inside a transaction, use savepoints. The one downside of database errors is that once one occurs inside a transaction, every subsequent statement fails. Ideally you won't need to roll back the entire transaction and start over, and a savepoint lets you avoid that.

The `nvarchar` data type has higher precedence than `varchar`. To compare them, SQL Server must implicitly convert the column to `nvarchar`, and that conversion rules out an index seek.

With certain collations, a seek is still possible. The `CONVERT_IMPLICIT` is moved into a residual predicate that is checked only against the rows the seek returns, rather than being evaluated for every row in the table during a scan. You are probably not using one of those collations.

The collation's influence can be shown by comparison. A SQL collation produces a scan. A Windows collation calls the internal function `GetRangeThroughConvert`, which lets the optimizer turn the operation into a seek.

In the Windows collation case, a compute scalar produces a set of values: a lower bound, an upper bound and a flags value. The seek predicate in the plan is an exclusive range between those bounds, so at first glance it would leave out `'1234'`. However, the flags value means that `'1234'` is in fact matched.

Note: how much of the index the seek covers depends on the length of the string in the equality comparison.

With a one-character predicate, for instance, the seek still reads every index value that begins with that character. A residual predicate then keeps only the exact matches. An empty-string predicate is worse still: with a zero-length prefix, the seek ends up reading the entire index.

It may sound odd, but errors raised by the database are a good thing. An error is simply a status report. It doesn't mean your application has to crash.

With an insert, there's an alternative course of action (update or do nothing), so it's reasonable to have syntax that lets you pick one. With an update, the only option is doing nothing. Why would SQL give you a way to request a specific behavior when there's nothing to choose between? Since database errors are useful, let the database do nothing and tell you why.

Finally, updating primary keys is bad practice. `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for inserts isn't meant to change primary key columns. It's the reverse: it's meant to update every column of a single record except the primary key ones.

The right approach depends on what your effects are doing.

First, suppose you need to attach event listeners when the component mounts and remove them when it unmounts, while another listener has to be removed and re-attached whenever a prop changes. Here, two separate effects are the better choice: each keeps its related setup and teardown logic together, and this also gives performance benefits.

Second, suppose you need to make an API call or run some other side effect whenever any value from a defined set of state or props changes. In that case, a single effect whose dependency array lists the relevant values is the better option.

Third, suppose you have side effects that respond to different sets of changes. Then separate those side effects into different effects, one for each set.

Which approach is right depends on what you're trying to do.

**Case 1:** You may have some event listeners that should be attached when the component first mounts and removed when it unmounts, plus a separate listener that has to be removed and re-attached whenever a certain prop changes. Here it's better to use two separate useEffect hooks. Each one keeps its related logic in one place, and you also gain performance.

**Case 2:** You want to fire an API call or another side effect whenever any value in a specific group of state or props changes. Here a single useEffect that lists all of those values as dependencies is the better choice.

**Case 3:** Different groups of changes each need their own side effect. Here you should split the side effects into separate useEffect hooks, one for each group.

`WORKDIR` sets the working directory for every command that follows it. `RUN cd`, on the other hand, doesn't affect any later `RUN` instructions.

Every `RUN` instruction starts a fresh shell with a fresh environment. Technically it also runs in a new container, though that usually isn't noticeable. How it starts is determined by the `ENV` and `WORKDIR` directives that appear earlier. So if a `RUN` step only changes directories, the change disappears when that shell exits, and the next step begins in whatever `WORKDIR` was most recently set for the image.

(The same reasoning explains why `RUN export` has no effect beyond its own Dockerfile instruction, and why `RUN .` or the non-standard `RUN source` won't leave environment variables set.)

WORKDIR changes the working directory for later commands, but RUN cd has no effect on subsequent RUN instructions. Each command runs in a new shell and a new environment (and technically a new container, though this rarely matters in practice). Any preceding SHELL and ENV directives affect how that shell starts. If a step only changes directories, the change is lost when the shell exits, and the next step starts in the image's most recent WORKDIR.

For the same reason, RUN cd doesn't persist beyond the current Dockerfile instruction. Neither does a non-standard directive, which also won't cause environment variables to be set.

What you have is a key in OpenSSH format, and what you need is one in PEM format. It seems counterintuitive, but the recommended conversion method is to change the key's password and write it out in a different format in the same step.

The command is:

```
ssh-keygen -p -N "" -m pem -f /path/to/key
```

This overwrites the existing file, so back up your current key first in case something goes wrong. The `-N ""` part sets an empty passphrase. I haven't tried this with a passphrase.

You shouldn't need to do anything to the public key.

For a complete explanation of the command, see the documentation for this option: https://man.openbsd.org/ssh-keygen#m

This error occurs when you index an object with a plain string. TypeScript sees that the string could be any value, not just one of the object's property names. To fix this, you can either add an index signature to the object's type, which tells TypeScript that any property name is allowed, or preferably narrow the type of the key so it can only be one of the object's actual properties. With the narrower type, only property names that exist on the object can be used.

You will also need to make a small change to your code. First assign the array to a temporary variable so TypeScript can infer its type.

If you get your data from an API and cannot check the properties at compile time, the only option is to add an index signature to your type.

Rather than doing that, I'd recommend changing the type of the key so that it can only be one of the object's properties.

Once you do this, only property names that actually exist on the object will be accepted.
